summary.title: A Neural Network in 13 lines of Python (Part 2 - Gradient Descent)
summary.one_liner: Gradient descent explained through a ball-in-a-bucket analogy and a short numpy neural network, showing how the alpha learning rate affects convergence, slow training, and divergence.
takeaways: Gradient descent updates each weight by subtracting the slope (error gradient), optionally scaled by alpha, until the slope reaches zero.
Too large a step (alpha too big) causes overshooting and divergence; too small a step causes very slow convergence or getting stuck in a local minimum.
Backpropagation does not optimize by itself; it computes error gradients that an optimizer such as gradient descent uses to update weights.
Multiple random starting states, such as many hidden nodes, help neural networks escape local minima.
A small 2-layer and 3-layer network in numpy demonstrates how alpha values from 0.001 to 1000 change training error over 60,000 iterations.
summary.summary: The post is a tutorial on gradient descent, starting with an intuitive ball-in-a-bucket analogy and a pseudocode version of the algorithm. It then covers common failure modes: divergence from steep slopes, local minima, and vanishing slopes, along with their fixes such as scaling steps by alpha and using random starts. The second half connects these ideas to neural networks by walking through a small 2-layer network's error surface and a 3-layer network trained on XOR-style data. The author runs experiments with alpha values from 0.001 to 1000 and explains the observed training error for each. The page is part of a series, and the author notes a planned follow-up on Dropout, DropConnect and Momentum.
